# Volume-preserving simplex truncation rules out low-order shape coercivity

Let T=conv(0,e_1,...,e_d), d>=2, V=|T|=1/d!, and
Gamma=(d/(d+1))^d. This note gives an explicit local signed BODY
perturbation of T, with equal volume, and separates three distances:
Hausdorff distance modulo every affine simplex, symmetric difference,
and halfspace-cap distance. Its depth excess is much smaller than the
square of its affine shape distance when d>=3.

The result rules out a proposed quadratic stability mechanism; it does
not prove that an exponent-d lower stability estimate holds. It does
not classify mixed extremizers or locate their maximum-depth points.

## 1. The convex perturbation and exact signed variation

For 0<epsilon<=1/[2(d+1)], set

    K_epsilon={x_i>=0, epsilon<=sum_i x_i<=1},
    e=epsilon^d, alpha=(1-e)^(-1/d),
    Ktilde_epsilon=alpha K_epsilon, delta=e/(1-e).

The removed part of T is epsilon T, of volume eV. Hence
|K_epsilon|=(1-e)V and |Ktilde_epsilon|=V exactly. All these are
full-dimensional convex bodies. Since (alpha epsilon)^d=delta<1,

    T outside Ktilde_epsilon = alpha epsilon T,
    Ktilde_epsilon outside T = alpha T outside T,       (1)

up to boundaries. The two sets in (1) both have volume delta V.
For every measurable H, including every closed halfspace, the exact
normalized signed variation is

    mu_(Ktilde)(H)-mu_T(H)
       = [|H intersect (alpha T outside T)|
          -|H intersect (alpha epsilon T)|]/V.          (2)

Consequently

    |Ktilde symmetric-difference T|/V=2delta,
    TV(mu_(Ktilde),mu_T)=delta,
    sup_(halfspaces H)|mu_(Ktilde)(H)-mu_T(H)|=delta.    (3)

The last equality is attained by H={sum x_i>=1}: its T mass is zero
and its Ktilde mass is exactly the outer shell delta. Thus cap distance
and total variation agree here, whereas the geometric boundary distance
will have order epsilon, not epsilon^d.

The true centroid can also be tracked exactly. With g=(1,...,1)/(d+1),

    g_(Ktilde)=alpha (1-epsilon^(d+1))/(1-epsilon^d) g.  (4)

This follows by subtracting the first moment of epsilon T before the
volume-restoring dilation. In particular its displacement is nonnegative
in every coordinate and ||g_(Ktilde)-g||_infinity<=delta. For this bound,
alpha<2 and Bernoulli gives alpha-1<=delta/d; hence the scalar factor
in (4) minus one is at most (2+1/d)delta, and division by d+1 is at most
delta for d>=2.

## 2. An exact upper bound on ordinary maximal-depth excess

The canonical d+1 centroid caps of T cover all continuous space and each
have volume Gamma V in T. Since K_epsilon subset T, each has no greater
absolute mass in K_epsilon. This gives the all-point upper bound

    Gamma <= D(Ktilde_epsilon)=D(K_epsilon)
          <= Gamma/(1-epsilon^d),
    0 <= D(Ktilde_epsilon)-Gamma <= Gamma delta.         (5)

The lower bound is ordinary Grunbaum applied at the true centroid.
The upper bound uses an actual finite cap cover, not a computation at
one proposed point. The body has the 2d distinct exposed vertices
e_i and epsilon e_i and is not a simplex. The independently proved
ordinary rigidity theorem in
`candidate e2c55c91458e1e8c` therefore makes
the lower inequality strict. Strictness is not needed for the rate
obstruction below. No weak-added-law first-variation theorem is used.

## 3. Distance from EVERY affine simplex is of order epsilon

Let dist_H,infinity be Hausdorff distance in the l_infinity norm and put

    c_d=(d-1)/[2d(2d-1)].

For every simplex S in R^d, including a degenerate one,

    dist_H,infinity(K_epsilon,S) >= c_d epsilon         (6)

whenever 0<epsilon<=1/d. This includes all affine images of T, with
arbitrary translations, shears, dilations and vertex choices.

Proof. Suppose the distance is rho<c_d epsilon. Every point p of S
satisfies p_i>=-rho and epsilon-d rho<=sum p_i<=1+d rho. Since e_i is
in K_epsilon, some vertex p^i of S has p^i_i>=1-rho. Its other coordinates
lie between -rho and (2d-1)rho, and p^i_i<=1+rho. Thus

    ||p^i-e_i||_infinity <=(2d-1)rho.

The d vertices p^i are distinct: rho<c_d epsilon<1/(2d), whereas a
vertex serving both i and j would require 1-rho<=(2d-1)rho.

For each i introduce the fixed linear exposing functional

    f_i(x)=x_i-2sum_j x_j,  ||f_i||_1=2d-1.

Its maximum on K_epsilon is -epsilon, attained at epsilon e_i. On
each of the d already assigned vertices p^j it is at most

    -1+(2d-1)^2 rho < -epsilon-(2d-1)rho.

The strict inequality follows from
rho<c_d epsilon<=(1-epsilon)/[2d(2d-1)], using epsilon<=1/d.
But Hausdorff support comparison requires max_S f_i>=-epsilon-(2d-1)rho.
Therefore all d functionals must achieve their maxima at the ONE
remaining simplex vertex p^0. If S has fewer than d+1 vertices this is
already impossible. Otherwise, with P=sum_j p^0_j, summing the required
inequalities gives

    -(2d-1)P >= -d epsilon-d(2d-1)rho,
    P <= d epsilon/(2d-1)+d rho.

The inclusion S subset K_epsilon+rho[-1,1]^d also gives P>=epsilon-d rho.
Combining these inequalities yields rho>=c_d epsilon, a contradiction.
This proves (6) without assuming an optimal approximating simplex exists.

For comparison, dist_H,infinity(K_epsilon,T)=epsilon/d exactly. Every
removed point can be moved into K_epsilon by adding the same amount,
at most epsilon/d, to all coordinates; the origin attains this distance.
Scaling (6) therefore gives

    alpha c_d epsilon
       <= inf_(all affine simplices S) dist_H,infinity(Ktilde_epsilon,S)
       <= alpha epsilon/d.                            (7)

Even if approximating simplices must have the same volume V, the lower
bound remains valid and T supplies an O_d(epsilon) upper bound:
dist_H,infinity(Ktilde,T)<=alpha epsilon/d+(alpha-1)<=4epsilon/d.

## 4. Affine-invariant distance and removal of affine modes

Define the simplex Banach--Mazur factor by the nested sandwich

    b(K)=inf{lambda>=1: S subset K subset p+lambda(S-p),
                          S a simplex, p in S}.

This is affine invariant. In the displayed sandwich for K_epsilon,
the diameter of S in l_infinity is at most one. Thus its Hausdorff
distance from K_epsilon is at most lambda-1. Formula (6) implies

    b(Ktilde_epsilon)-1=b(K_epsilon)-1>=c_d epsilon.     (8)

An explicit matching upper order is obtained from the centroid homothet
S=g+a(T-g), where a=1-(d+1)epsilon/d. This simplex lies in K_epsilon:
its minimum coordinate sum is epsilon. Also K_epsilon subset T, and
T=g+a^(-1)(S-g). Therefore

    b(Ktilde_epsilon)-1 <= [(d+1)epsilon/d]
                                /[1-(d+1)epsilon/d]
                         <=2(d+1)epsilon/d.            (9)

The chosen epsilon range ensures the final denominator is at least
one half. These are shape distances after ALL affine simplex choices
have already been factored out.

One may additionally translate Ktilde to give it the EXACT same centroid
g as T. This preserves its volume, depth and distance to the entire
affine simplex orbit, as well as b(K). Its cap distance from T remains
at most (1+d d!)delta. Indeed translate by v=g-g_(Ktilde), use (3),
and note that a translated T halfspace changes normalized mass by at
most d d! ||v||_infinity. To verify the latter bound, normalize its
normal to have maximum coordinate magnitude one, integrate first along
such a coordinate, and bound the other d-1 coordinate ranges by [0,1].
The threshold changes by at most d||v||_infinity and V=1/d!.

Combining (5), (7) and (8), for EVERY exponent 0<p<d the ratios

    [D(Ktilde_epsilon)-Gamma]
       /[inf_S dist_H,infinity(Ktilde_epsilon,S)]^p,
    [D(Ktilde_epsilon)-Gamma]/[b(Ktilde_epsilon)-1]^p

tend to zero. In particular no positive uniform quadratic coercivity
constant can hold near the simplex for d>=3. For d=2 this example rules
out exponents below two, but does not decide quadratic coercivity.
No exponent-d lower bound is asserted in any dimension.

## 5. The perturbation is compatible with fixed neighboring fibers

This is not an inadmissible deformation of an isolated artificial fiber.
Let A=g+(T-g)/2, of volume 2^(-d)V, and put A at integer bases -1,+1
and Ktilde_epsilon at base zero. Take their actual Cayley hull. The
endpoint fibers are exactly A by exposedness. The middle is exactly
Ktilde_epsilon because A is strictly contained in it.

For the last assertion, every A point has positive coordinates, its
coordinate sum is between d/[2(d+1)] and (2d+1)/[2(d+1)], while the
middle has lower and upper sums alpha epsilon and alpha. The stated
epsilon range, alpha<2<=d (strict at d=2), gives strict lower inclusion;
the upper sum is strictly below 1<=alpha. Thus all sampled Minkowski
conditions hold with strict inclusion, all three fibers stay positive,
and the source is a full-dimensional convex body. The middle base is
nonexposed. There is no claim here about which point globally maximizes
its mixed depth; in this particular small-neighbor realization the
middle's own volume already exceeds half the total for d>=2.

The example shows why a body-deformation argument cannot pay arbitrary
neighboring cap losses of order epsilon^p, p<d, solely from a supposed
coercive ordinary depth excess at Hausdorff/Banach--Mazur scale epsilon.
Cap distance and symmetric difference instead have order epsilon^d and
must be tracked separately. The exact ordinary depth law, if derived,
can refine (5); it is not needed for this obstruction.

The companion exact verifier is
`../assets/pk-nov6/computations/verify_simplex_truncation_affine_distance_obstruction.py`.

## 6. The exact leading order from the independently audited depth law

The subsequent theorem
`candidate 3795aff5f3322d52`,
independently checked in `unshared historical review/context (not an accepted premise)`,
now supplies the matching leading order for this SAME path:

    D(Ktilde_epsilon)-Gamma
       =[Gamma-1/(d+1)] epsilon^d+O_d(epsilon^(2d)).

Its coefficient is strictly positive for d>=2. Thus the order epsilon^d
in (5) is exact, rather than merely an upper bound. This refinement does
not alter the all-affine distance proof or imply a general stability
theorem for other convex perturbations.
